name: Professional Learning That Works
title: Professional Learning That Works
answer: Professional learning about AI should focus on pedagogy, not just technical skill. The book argues that teachers' knowledge of how to teach with AI predicts student outcomes better than technical knowledge alone. It also says professional learning must be ongoing and connected to real teaching work.

sections.body: This idea says that AI professional learning often overemphasizes how to operate tools. The problem is that technical skill by itself does not reliably improve teaching or students' views of AI. Research in the text suggests that knowing how to teach with AI matters more. The text also says confidence grows when teachers apply AI to real teaching tasks. The text puts pedagogy ahead of technology.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, professional learning should look like the real work teachers do. For secondary teachers, the text points to knowledge of how to teach with AI rather than technical skill alone. For middle school science teachers, case based learning moved from simple to messy cases of AI in teaching, and the messier cases pushed teachers to apply what they learned. Teachers who applied AI to their own lessons improved more than those who studied tools without that context. The text also says professional learning should be ongoing, with time to try tools, reflect, and share with colleagues, and professional learning communities are a fitting setting for this work.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text presents this idea as supported by research. A study of 46 secondary teachers and more than 2,800 students found that the predictor of students' views of AI's value for society and their interest in learning about it was teachers' pedagogical knowledge for AI, not their technical skill (Shen et al., 2026). Technical knowledge on its own slightly reduced how students viewed AI's social value. A study of 325 teachers in 26 countries found that technical skill led to confident AI use in teaching only by way of teachers' knowledge of how to use technology for teaching (Mohebi & ElSayary, 2026). In a program with middle school science teachers, working through realistic teaching cases involving AI, moving from simple to messy, improved teachers' AI literacy, and the messier cases prompted teachers to apply their learning (Ding et al., 2024), and the text notes the study was small but its approach fits the broader research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on this idea. It says a district that provides a single training and then expects change to last will be let down. It also notes that technical knowledge alone slightly lowered students' views of AI's social value, so tool training by itself carries a risk. The case based learning study was small, so that finding should not be treated as settled. The text does not name specific decisions that stay with a person, but it places teachers' own lessons, reflection, and sharing at the center, which keeps professional judgment with teachers.
